content: 1. Extended supervision was implemented, incorporating mentoring and regular follow-up to ensure adherence to best practices. 2. Prevention was established as a top priority. The Ministry of Health (MOH) emphasized the prevention and reduction of healthcare-associated infections (HCAIs) within the national infection prevention and control (IPC) program. Investments were made in surveillance, outbreak investigations, laboratory research, and other preventive measures. 3. Monitoring and accountability mechanisms were strengthened. Discussions were held to integrate evaluation tools into routine hospital monitoring across Tanzania and within existing quality improvement programs. 4. Hygiene committees were established in all healthcare facilities and treatment centers located in cholera hotspots in Cameroon. These committees consisted of well-trained, multidisciplinary teams capable of responding to outbreaks within 72 hours. 5. Community partnerships were reinforced, and adherence to hand hygiene guidelines in healthcare facilities improved. Disease surveillance activities were also enhanced at all levels. 6. In treatment centers, wards were refurbished to include isolation areas, increase bed spacing, and improve natural ventilation and lighting. Handwashing materials were provided, and disinfection practices for wards and patient transport vehicles were improved. 7. At the community level, sensitization efforts led to better practices in disinfection, household water treatment, and proper disposal of human waste and food hygiene. 8. Despite these efforts, the risk of cholera resurgence in Cameroon remains high due to its proximity to endemic regions. Continuous community education on hygiene practices is essential, though behavior change and limited funding remain challenges. 9. In Mali, following a 2012 cholera outbreak, a national assessment revealed significant inadequacies in healthcare facilities, including poor water supply and open defecation. An intersectoral task force was established to coordinate efforts and raise awareness about the importance of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) in healthcare facilities. 10. Mali adopted a minimum national WASH package and conducted training programs, which were rolled out in several regions. By 2017, WASH indicators were integrated into routine national health system monitoring. 11. Over 200 healthcare facilities in Mali benefited from infrastructure upgrades, addressing all eight practical steps outlined in the WASH improvement framework. Communities were empowered to hold facilities accountable for better services and efficient resource allocation. 12. In India, the Kayakalp Award Scheme was launched in 2015 to improve cleanliness, hygiene, waste management, and infection control in public healthcare facilities. Facilities achieving at least 70% of the indicators received cash awards, with over 500 facilities recognized. 13. In Madhya Pradesh, India, a focused program aimed to improve WASH in maternity settings across nine districts, creating infection-free environments in nearly 200 facilities and benefiting over 120,000 newborns. 14. Mobile applications facilitated regular monitoring and identified key needs, such as low-cost interventions like hand hygiene and cleaning. By 2017, healthcare facilities in Madhya Pradesh saw significant improvements in WASH protocols, access to functional water services, toilets, and handwashing stations. 15. In Kenya, researchers adapted the WASH FIT tool to create the WASH Facility Survey Tool (WASH-FaST) for assessing larger, more complex healthcare facilities. This tool helped prioritize WASH actions and identify quick wins, such as increasing waste bins and improving segregation practices. 16. The WHO/UNICEF knowledge portal for WASH in healthcare facilities provides resources, case studies, assessment tools, and training materials. It is regularly updated to support ongoing improvements and innovation in WASH practices globally.
